From upside-down houses to furniture built for giants, Jean-François Fourtou's sculpture park in the Moroccan city of Marrakech turns childhood memories into a surreal, immersive experience.

What if you could step back into your childhood and see the world exactly as you did then? In Marrakech, one French artist is doing just that by presenting upside-down houses, giant furniture and surreal, wildly imaginative sculptures.

At Ramakech, an outdoor sculpture park located on the outskirts of the Moroccan city, visitors can immerse themselves in the work of Jean-François Fourtou, whose sculptures draw heavily on memories of childhood, family and the way we experience the world as children.

Perhaps the star attraction of the 11-hectare park is 'The house that fell from the sky'. Created in 2010, the house is completely inverted, with furniture, windows and bathroom fixtures turned upside down, giving the impression that, as the title suggests, it's come and crash landed onto its roof.

"'The house that fell from the sky' is the house where my grandfather died more than 30 years ago. He was a very important figure throughout my childhood, inspiring me and shaping the way I express myself artistically, including the way I do today. So, I wanted to pay tribute to him," says Fourtou.

He adds: "To me, it is as if he had sent this house back to me from the sky. It was a small rented house in Charente-Maritime, where he used to spend his summers."

Childhood is a theme that runs throughout the park, with many of Fourtou's installations drawing on the strange, exaggerated way the world can feel when you're a child.

His 'Giant House' is one of the first installations he created for the site, featuring oversized furniture and everyday objects, from chairs and tables to notebooks, pens and clothing. Visitors are encouraged to release their inner child and climb, sit and interact with the objects.

"I wanted to recapture the feelings I had when I was four years old, staying at my great-grandmother’s house in a village in the south of France. There was barely any running water, no bathroom, and everything was very rustic. I have wonderful memories of that place, and I wanted to rediscover those childhood sensations," explains Fourtou.

Elsewhere, there's also a wonderfully whimsical take on the natural world, with sculptures of farmers and gardeners with enormous heads inspired by vegetables and plants. They can be found scattered throughout the park, tending the land, climbing trees and resting in the shade. There are also a few oversized ants to be found crawling around the landscape.

As Fourtou puts it: "Art is something deeply emotional, and that is what I seek to convey through my work. For me, it is certainly a form of therapy, not a nostalgia for childhood, but rather a way of understanding, expressing and reconnecting with important fundamental values."

He began transforming the site into a space for his artwork in 1999, with the park opening to the public in 2024. It now attracts around 5,000 visitors every year.

Announcements on payments to Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia from the EU’s €6 billion regional Growth Plan are expected shortly. Plans to extend the EU’s roaming-free mobile phone regime to the region are also advancing.

As we saw at our own Euronews Enlargement Summit earlier this month, the prospect of a bigger EU is more tangible than it has been in years. But with French presidential elections looming next spring, the political window for enlargement may not stay open indefinitely.

Something rotten in the state of Denmark?

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s hardline approach to migration is setting the cat among the pigeons in her European political family, with Socialist MEPs gearing up for a showdown over her increasingly controversial rhetoric.

The latest flashpoint was a Danish podcast last week in which Frederiksen declared her opposition to a “great replacement of the population”, language critics say echoes the far-right conspiracy theory. She also spoke of Denmark’s “original tribe, which is ethnically Danish” and the need to preserve a strong majority culture.

“This podcast was a disaster,” one S&D MEP told Vincenzo Genovese.

Portuguese and German MEPs voiced their objections at a stormy group meeting in Strasbourg on Monday, prompting S&D chief Iratxe García Pérez to promise a formal debate.

How far is too far? Frederiksen has long been an awkward fit for Europe’s centre-left. Her restrictive migration policies have gone hand in hand with the electoral decline of Denmark’s once-powerful far right.

But her latest initiative – teaming up with Austria, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to establish a migrant return hub in Rwanda – directly contradicts the S&D’s opposition to such facilities.

“For now, no one is taking her side,” a senior Socialist lawmaker told Euronews.

No disciplinary action is expected, and any sanctions would be a matter for the wider Party of European Socialists. But the impending showdown exposes a deeper dilemma for Europe’s centre-left: how far can Social Democrats accommodate demands for tougher migration policies without compromising their own principles?

Holding the centre. The European Parliament’s centrist chiefs – Manfred Weber, Iratxe García Pérez and Valérie Hayer – met in Strasbourg to hammer out a coalition agreement for the second half of the parliamentary term. Not a single molecule. EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Euronews’ On the Record that Europe will never return to Russian energy, whatever Washington and Moscow agree. Even if peace brings an end to sanctions, the EU’s gas import ban will remain. Meanwhile, he warns consumers to brace for a difficult winter.

COP out? Brussels is drawing up plans to overhaul UN climate summits after the COP31 fiasco in Antalya. The Commission wants more transparency, streamlined negotiations and an end to a system where one country can block nearly 200 others. Meanwhile, smaller coalitions of willing countries could drive the fossil fuel transition.

Asylum ruling. The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled on Tuesday that Poland and Latvia exposed to inhuman or degrading treatment individuals who have tried to enter their territory from Belarus in 2021. The ruling could set a precedent for similar cases of state-sponsored pressure, such as the mass arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta from Morocco last July.

Space invaders. NATO chief Mark Rutte has vowed to defend allies against threats in space following German media reports that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite within weeks. Moscow denies the allegations. Such a weapon could devastate satellite networks underpinning global communications and navigation, violating the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

Lessons unlearnt. Twenty years after Alexander Litvinenko’s murder in London, his widow Marina told Euronews that the West’s feeble response emboldened Vladimir Putin, paving the way for Russia’s war in Ukraine. She warns Europe against negotiating from a position of weakness and insists justice ultimately requires putting Putin’s regime on trial.

The provisional quotas, which also cover other major exporters including Japan, Turkey and Britain, follow an EU-China trade agreement in October. Longer-term restrictions are in the pipeline as Brussels seeks to rein in its whopping €360 billion trade deficit with Beijing.

Quantum leap. Determined not to repeat the mistakes of the AI race, Brussels unveils its Quantum Act today, aiming to make Europe a global powerhouse in the technology by 2030. The plans favour European companies in public procurement. But there’s a security imperative too: quantum computers could render existing encryption obsolete, leaving everything from banking to government communications exposed.

Almost one in three Europeans say they cannot afford the upfront cost of installing a heat pump.

For Europeans worried about how much it will cost to heat their homes this winter, switching to a heat pump is an attractive prospect.

That is, if they can get past the cost of installing one.

Interest in heat pumps is growing across Europe – especially in households struggling to pay their energy bills - according to a survey of 6,000 people in France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland and the UK.

But almost one in three said they can’t afford the upfront installation costs, making it the most cited obstacle to making the switch.

How much can heat pumps save on energy bills?

Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume. Once they are installed, they can have a big impact on your bottom line.

According to the IEA, heat pumps are cheaper to run than gas boilers in almost every EU country, offering annual energy savings of up to €800.

When used effectively, air-source heat pumps could heat homes for as little as €2.20 on a typical winter day, according to British property developer Barratt Redrow.

Jean-Paul Harreman, director at market intelligence provider Montel, says that, even in very cold weather, “the efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler.”

How much does it cost to install a heat pump?

Making the switch still requires investment. Installing a heat pump can cost several thousands euros more than a gas boiler. Often, the installation costs as much as the equipment itself, if not more.

In the UK, the average cost of installing an air-source heat pump was about €15,000 in 2025 – five times the cost of installing a new gas boiler.

And the prices are not uniform across the continent, either. In Germany, it can cost up to €40,000. Much of that difference boils down to the equipment, Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford, explained in a recent analysis.

Germany’s heat pump market is dominated by more expensive European manufacturers, while cheaper brands – including some sourced from Asia – are more widely available in the UK, France and the Netherlands.

Stricter installation requirements and taxation are also factors. For example, Germany charges 19 per cent VAT on heat pump installations, while the UK scrapped VAT on them in 2022. Some homes may also need to have their radiators replaced or their electrical systems upgraded, which adds to the bill.

But labour, Rosenow added, is not a major factor in prices. “We expected labour costs to make a big difference but were surprised to find that they didn’t.”

That leaves room for installation prices to come down as equipment becomes cheaper.

How to lower heat pump prices

There are many ways to mitigate the costs, however.

Across Europe, governments are offering grants, tax breaks and low-interest loans to encourage homeowners to switch to greener heating.

In England and Wales, eligible homeowners can receive a grant of around €8,500 towards installation. France, Germany and Italy also offer financial assistance to make the switch.

But for people already struggling to pay their bills, even reduced prices may be unaffordable.

Three-quarters of respondents in the poll, commissioned by the European Climate Foundation, said rising living and energy costs have affected their budgets, and two-thirds expect to heat some rooms less this winter. Yet fewer than half say they are likely to invest in home improvements or energy-saving equipment.

Paying subsidies in advance rather than reimbursing after heat pumps are installed is one possible solution. Nearly six in 10 respondents in Verian’s survey say they would back such a measure. In fact, the idea received majority support in all six countries.

Homeowners can also save money by shopping around. The UK’s Energy Saving Trust recommends getting quotes from at least three qualified installers, as well as having your home assessed to ensure you are not paying for a more powerful heat pump than you need.

Choosing a speciality electricity tariff or installing solar panels to generate some of the electricity needed to run your heat pump can also offset costs and lower bills.

Even if Europeans are warming up to heat pumps, the need to “[make] the financial benefits clearer and more immediate for households”, as the Verian study revealed, might be growing just as quickly.

Spain's economy is forecast to grow more than twice as fast as the eurozone's this year, but average pay still buys less than it did in 2009. Rising housing and food costs are putting household budgets under pressure ahead of Sunday's election.

Average wages in Spain were still below their 2009 peak last year after being adjusted for inflation, even as the economy continued to outgrow most of its European peers.

Spain's economy is forecast to grow by 2.6% this year, more than twice the eurozone's projected 1.2%, according to the European Commission. But that growth has brought only modest gains in average real pay since Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took office in 2018.

The gap between a fast-growing economy and what households can afford has become a campaign issue ahead of Sunday's snap election. Sánchez has pointed to Spain's strong growth while acknowledging voters' concerns about the cost of living. His main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, has accused the government of doing too little and pledged to cut personal income tax in his first year in office.

Five figures show how wages, food prices and housing costs have shaped what Spaniards can afford.

2009

That was the peak for Spain's inflation-adjusted average annual wage in the OECD series. In 2025, the average was €35,121, about 1% below the 2009 peak of €35,533 and about 5% above its 2018 level.

Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labour force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.

“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”

Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.

45%

While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, food prices also rose substantially, by 45% between 2015 and 2025, according to AP. The government has at various points cut VAT on food, subsidised energy and provided financial support to households.

Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”

Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticising Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.

Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.

“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

43%

House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.

Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.

Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

Homebuilding fell sharply after the 2008 financial crisis ended a construction boom. Large investors bought property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation in later years. Sánchez and Feijóo have both promised financial help for first-time buyers if elected.

Two-thirds

About two-thirds of people aged 18 to 34 in Spain were still living with their parents in 2025, according to figures from Spain's National Statistics Institute. Among 26- to 34-year-olds who lived with their parents, 47.3% said the main reason was that they could not afford to rent or buy a home.

Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas. Population growth has increased demand, while the spread of short-term tourist lets on platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com has reduced the supply of homes available to long-term renters in some areas.

1 in 4

That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidised or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.

In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.

“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”

"During the holiday season, the lights along Oxford Street and Regent Street, elaborately decorated storefronts and Winter Wonderland transform the city," TUI Musement said.

It also added that an iconic landmark like the Thames offers visitors river cruises with the perfect vantage point to see the city illuminated.

In second place comes the French capital Paris. The City of Love received a total of 252,800 Christmas and New Year’s related searches over the past year, which comes amid the run-up to the Champs-Élysées Christmas market revival.

After a decade-long absence, the Parisian holiday attraction now features 200 exhibitors housed in wooden chalets between the Rond-Point des Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde.

TUI Musement described its historic centre transforming "into a scene straight out of a Christmas story, with the traditional market at East Princes Street Gardens, fairground rides and festive storefront displays".

Luxembourg's average full-time salary was more than five times Bulgaria's in 2025. Once local prices are taken into account, Greece ranks last, and Luxembourg's average salary buys about three times as much.

The average annual full-time adjusted salary in the EU was €41,464 in 2025, according to Eurostat figures published on 6 November 2026.

The gap between countries was wide. In Luxembourg, the average was more than five times as high as in Bulgaria.

To make pay easier to compare across countries, Eurostat expresses part-time salaries as full-time equivalents.

So, which countries had the highest and lowest average salaries? How do the rankings change when purchasing power is taken into account? And how do experts explain the differences?

Luxembourg pays the most

Across the 26 EU countries in Eurostat's ranking, average gross full-time adjusted salaries ranged from €16,201 in Bulgaria to €85,609 in Luxembourg, more than five times Bulgaria's figure.

Among the remaining countries, Denmark (€73,500), Ireland (€64,387), Belgium (€61,984) and Austria (€60,727) had the highest average salaries, rounding out the top five, all above €60,000.

Germany leads the 'Big Four'

Among the EU's 'Big Four' economies, Germany had the highest average salary at €56,360. France was just above the EU average at €44,734.

Gross full-time pay was much lower in the bloc's third- and fourth-largest economies, at €34,213 in Italy and €35,125 in Spain.

Other countries above the EU average included Finland (€50,960) and Sweden (€49,622).

At the bottom of the list, Bulgaria has the lowest average salary at €16,201. Greece (€18,772) and Hungary (€20,138) follow. Romania (€20,818), Slovakia (€21,661) and Latvia (€22,688) are also among the lowest.

These are gross salaries, and net earnings or incomes can vary because of differences in taxes and social contributions between countries.

The pay gap narrows once local prices are taken into account

The purchasing power standard (PPS) is a unit used to compare what money can buy across countries. It removes the effect of price differences across countries, so one PPS buys the same amount of goods and services everywhere.

The gap narrows when salaries are adjusted for differences in household prices, according to Euronews Business calculations using Eurostat data.

The highest average salary is about three times the lowest, compared with more than five times in euros.

Luxembourg still ranks first with 65,106 PPS. Bulgaria moves up two places to 24th, while Greece ranks last with 21,486 PPS.

The ranking also changes substantially. Slovenia moves above the EU average, while Sweden and the bloc's second-largest economy, France, fall below it.

Poland and Lithuania each rise three places. Austria moves from fifth to second place. Denmark falls from second to fourth, and Ireland from third to sixth.

Several Central and Eastern European countries move up in the PPS ranking. Romania climbs from 23rd to 18th place, the biggest rise at five places.

Estonia has the biggest drop, falling from 16th to 21st place.

Why do salaries differ so much?

According to experts, the main reasons are differences in economic development and productivity.

"By and large, of course, the main reason for the differences in wages across European countries is the different levels of economic development and productivity, and the output created by workers," Jaan Masso, associate professor in applied econometrics at the University of Tartu, told Euronews Business.

Štěpán Jurajda, professor at CERGE-EI in Prague, pointed to similar factors. "The main reasons for the large gaps in salaries across European countries include different endowments of physical and human capital (education) and different productivity (including institutions, effective regulation, R&D policies etc.)," he told Euronews Business.

Labour market rules also play a significant role. Masso said minimum wages and collective agreements affect how equal wages are. He noted that "typically wages are much more equal in the Scandinavian countries".

Why are prices higher in rich countries?

Jurajda explained that richer countries usually have higher prices. "A basic empirical fact is that as countries become richer, their price level rises," he said.

Masso gave an example from the services sector. In some services, productivity cannot rise much. "One still needs similar time to cut hair," he said. So in high-wage countries, higher labour costs lead to higher prices for services.

"Naturally, for people living in a particular country, the price-adjusted figure is more relevant," Masso added.

Jurajda urged caution when reading the rankings. "In general, small PPP-adjusted differences should not be interpreted as precise country rankings," he said.

Is the East-West gap closing?

Malte Lübker, a wage expert at the Institute of Economic and Social Research (WSI) at the Hans Böckler Foundation, said the gap has narrowed.

"In the past, employers in high-wage countries have often pointed at lower wages in Eastern Europe to call for domestic wage restraint. However, the gap has closed considerably over time," he told Euronews Business.

Lübker said that this also affects migration. "When you adjust for purchasing power, taking up a job in Germany is no longer such an attractive proposition for Polish workers," he said.

What do full-time salaries not show?

Adjusting salaries to full-time equivalents makes comparisons easier. But experts say it has limitations.

"Converting wage data into full-time equivalents is, of course, a useful statistical technique. However, we should not forget that full-time work might not be readily available," Lübker said.

"For others, primarily women, part-time employment is the only way to reconcile work and care responsibilities. This means that full-time wages are an imperfect proxy for living standards."

Masso noted that part-time work varies a lot across Europe. In many Eastern European countries, full-time work has been the norm, while in the Netherlands part-time work is very common.

Experts also point out that averages can hide large differences within a country. Masso said that in Luxembourg, "the high average might be affected by a smaller number of very highly paid jobs, e.g., in the financial sector".

Alongside his wife Carla Bruni, the ex-French president will face court in late 2027, accused of conspiracy and hiding witness tampering over alleged Libyan funding of his 2007 campaign.

Just six days before the appeal court is due to announce its decision in the case over the alleged Libyan financing of the 2007 presidential campaign, Nicolas Sarkozy already has another date with the courts.

Together with his wife, singer Carla Bruni, the former president is being sent for trial before the Paris criminal court in the case over the possibly paid-for retraction by Franco-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, a source close to the case said on Tuesday, 24 November.

All those placed under formal investigation in this case, including Mimi Marchand, "high priestess of the paparazzi," are being sent before the courts.

Nicolas Sarkozy and his partner will be tried for "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised gang" and "concealment of witness tampering".

Mimi Marchand will be tried for "witness tampering," "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised gang" and "with a view to preparing acts of corruption of foreign judicial personnel". Their trial is expected to take place from 3 November to 2 December 2027.

The defendants face a maximum sentence of ten years in prison and a fine of 150,000 euros.

The U-turns of Ziad Takieddine, key witness in the Libyan case

This new chapter in the former head of state's legal troubles is linked to the case that had earned him a five-year prison sentenceafter a guilty plea for criminal conspiracy. He had been released from prison after twenty days pending his appeal.

One of the main complainants in this case was Franco-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, who died in Lebanon last year. In 2016, he said he had helped deliver up to five million euros in cash from Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi to Nicolas Sarkozy and the former president's chief of staff in 2006 and 2007.

But in November 2020, Ziad Takieddine suddenly backtracked on his incriminating statements in an interview with French media before changing his mind once again.

This gave rise to allegations that Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife had called on "the queen of the paparazzi", Mimi Marchand, to pay this key witness to retract his statements, something they have always denied.

Carla Bruni is suspected in particular of having requested a clandestine phone line at the end of 2019 so she could communicate with Mimi Marchand about the Ziad Takieddine case.

Numerous run-ins with the law

In the case of the alleged financing of the 2007 presidential campaign, Nicolas Sarkozy became the first former French president to be jailed.

But the former occupant of the Élysée has also been definitively convicted in two other cases: the first linked to overspending during his unsuccessful 2012 election campaign, the second for later trying to obtain favours from a judge.

Mimi Marchand, for her part, was given an 18-month suspended prison sentence last year for blackmailing a television presenter, who feared she would publish images of her daughter leaving a police station.

A Swedish research team set out to identify who could benefit most from taking vitamin D supplements.

Low vitamin D in the summertime may be a bigger red flag for your health than in the winter months, a new study has found.

Vitamin D helps the body regulate calcium and phosphate in the body, keeping our bones, teeth and muscles healthy. Most of it comes from sunlight, while people can also get some vitamin D from foods such as oily fish, eggs and some mushrooms. Millions of Europeans also take vitamin D supplements, though randomised trials have largely failed to show that routine supplementation improves health or boosts longevity.

Researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden wondered if seasonal swings in vitamin D levels might help explain why. In Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere, people build up stores of vitamin D in their fat during the sunny summer months, and they may draw on those reserves as their vitamin D levels naturally fall in the darker winter months.

“We need to better understand who truly needs vitamin D supplementation,” the researchers wrote.

To find out, the researchers analysed vitamin D levels in the blood of more than 12,000 older people in Sweden. They split participants into groups based on whether their blood was drawn in summer, from July to September, or in winter, from January to March.

People with low vitamin D levels in summer were more likely to fracture a bone or die over the next 11 years, on average, than those with high summer levels. Meanwhile, people who had low vitamin D levels in the winter months were not at increased risk of bone fracture or death, according to the study, which was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

People were considered to have low vitamin D if their blood concentration was below 40 nanomoles per litre (nmo/L) and high levels if it was above 80 nmol/L.

The findings suggest summer could be the best time to test vitamin D levels. That could help doctors identify people who are chronically low and could benefit the most from supplements, the researchers said.

“We should think carefully about when we measure vitamin D,” the researchers wrote. “Winter measurements are heavily influenced by seasonal variation, whereas low vitamin D levels during summer are more likely to reflect persistently low vitamin D status and a higher risk of adverse health outcomes.”

This was an observational study, meaning it cannot show whether low vitamin D levels cause bone fractures or early death. It was also conducted mainly in white Swedish people, so the results may not directly apply to other groups. Still, the findings held even after the researchers accounted for age, sex, body size and other factors.

The researchers said more randomised trials are needed to identify the potential health benefits of supplements, ideally focused on people with low vitamin D levels in the summer.

North Korea has ordered Switzerland to shut its newly opened diplomatic office in Pyongyang and given its head 48 hours to leave the country in retaliation for Swiss sanctions on a children's camp linked to Russia.

State news agency KCNA reported on Wednesday that a senior Foreign Ministry official called in Astier Sylvain, who leads the Swiss mission, and handed him a written demand for the office's closure. Pyongyang declared him persona non grata.

The move follows a warning on Tuesday from Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un and one of the regime's leading foreign policy voices, who called the sanctions an "open hostile act" that violated North Korean sovereignty.

The expulsion comes five weeks after Benn restarted operations in Pyongyang.

A rare Western channel under strain

Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.

KCNA said the talks covered "promoting dialogue and cooperation." The office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, and Bern said it would help build direct contact with North Korean officials.

Switzerland has had diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and remains one of the few Western states to keep a line open. Its development agency ran a cooperation office in Pyongyang from 1997, focused largely on humanitarian work, until it closed in March 2020, when North Korea sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Swiss Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that it wanted to keep channels of dialogue open despite political differences.

It stressed that reopening the office is separate from its sanctions policy, whether UN measures tied to North Korea's nuclear programme or the EU sanctions Switzerland has adopted over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The camp at the centre of the dispute

Bern recently added the Songdowon International Children's Camp, in the coastal city of Wonsan, to its sanctions list over Russia's war in Ukraine.

Swiss authorities say the facility is part of programmes that bring Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory to North Korea, where they are exposed to pro-Russian propaganda.

The UK sanctioned the camp in May, and the EU followed in September, freezing its assets and banning financial dealings with it. Given North Korea's minimal financial links with Europe, the practical effect of these measures is uncertain.

Kim Yo Jong said the camp serves "legitimate" cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. She did not directly respond to Western allegations that abducted Ukrainian children have been sent there for re-education.

North Korea has moved steadily closer to Russia during the war, supplying thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support Vladimir Putin's invasion, possibly in return for aid and military technology.

Closer relations with Moscow and Beijing have underpinned Kim Jong Un's more assertive foreign policy as he seeks to end the country's isolation and present it as part of a bloc opposed to Washington.
